That band sits inside the EU 865-868 MHz band, so EU-tuned inlays fit India, but US 902-928 MHz stock reads short; HF NFC and MIFARE run at 13.56 MHz and are unaffected. Express air reaches Mumbai, Delhi, Bangalore, and Chennai in 5-7 business days; RFID readers need WPC ETA before customs clearance; and because India has no free-trade agreement with China, Basic Customs Duty plus IGST apply on import (confirm the exact landed figure on your quote). sections.title: Get the band right: India's 865-867 MHz under the WPC/DoT
sections.intro: The single most expensive mistake in cross-border RFID sourcing is band mismatch. India's UHF RAIN band is 865-867 MHz, de-licensed for RFID by the WPC wing of the Department of Telecommunications under GSR 564(E) at up to 1 W transmitter power / 4 W ERP with a 200 kHz carrier. Here is the useful twist: 865-867 MHz sits inside the EU 865-868 MHz band, so an EU-tuned inlay works well in India — while a US 902-928 MHz inlay reads short. If you are new to frequency planning, start with our [LF vs HF vs UHF guide](/blog/rfid-frequencies-lf-hf-uhf-explained/) or the [RAIN RFID explainer](/guides/rain-rfid-explained/).

sections.title: Indian compliance: WPC ETA, TEC, BIS, and data
sections.intro: Two questions decide whether a shipment clears cleanly into India — radio approval and data handling. Below is the honest map for China-sourced RFID; for the credential-level stack, our [access-control solution](/solutions/rfid-access-control/) covers readers and encoding, and our [brand-authentication solution](/solutions/nfc-brand-authentication/) covers NFC anti-counterfeit.

callout.text: The WPC ETA obligation sits on the reader, the intentional radiator — not on the passive tags and cards we supply. Order 865-867 MHz-tuned inlays, pair them with a WPC-ETA reader from your PACS or RTLS vendor, and keep the ETA number on file for customs.

sections.title: Landed cost: HS 8523.52, no India-China FTA, BCD + IGST
sections.intro: The unit price is the headline; the landed cost is the story. India has no free-trade agreement with China, so there is no preferential tariff to claim — the plot is Basic Customs Duty, IGST, and the Incoterm that decides who pays them. Our [RFID RFP template](/blog/rfid-rfp-template-questions-suppliers/) shows the quote-comparison math in full; the short version is below.

dataHighlight.heading: No India-China FTA, so standard import duty and IGST apply — quoted, not guessed
dataHighlight.text: RFID cards and tags fall in the HS 8523.52 ("smart cards") family. Because there is no India-China free-trade agreement, imports get no tariff preference: Basic Customs Duty (BCD) plus Integrated GST (IGST) are levied at the border. The exact BCD and IGST depend on the precise 8-digit HS classification and the current Union Budget, so we quote the landed figure against your specification rather than publish a rate that would soon be stale. Many Indian buyers prefer to import on their own IEC (Importer-Exporter Code) so they can reclaim IGST as input credit — in which case FOB or CIF suits better than DDP. Confirm the exact duty and IGST with your customs broker.

faq.question: Which UHF band do your RFID tags use for India?
faq.answer: India's de-licensed UHF RFID band is 865-867 MHz, allocated by the WPC (Wireless Planning & Coordination) wing of the Department of Telecommunications at up to 1 W transmitter power, 4 W ERP, and 200 kHz carrier bandwidth (GSR 564(E)). We tune passive inlays for 865-867 MHz. Because that band sits inside the EU 865-868 MHz band, EU-tuned stock also fits India — but US 902-928 MHz inlays read short and are not a drop-in. We use broadband Gen2 chips (Impinj Monza, NXP UCODE) that cover the full 860-960 MHz range, with the antenna tuned to the Indian band. HF NFC and access cards at 13.56 MHz are global and unaffected.

faq.question: Do RFID readers need WPC approval, and will you clear Indian customs?
faq.answer: Yes for readers: an RFID reader is an intentional radiator and needs WPC ETA (Equipment Type Approval) before it can be imported or sold in India — customs may hold radio equipment that lacks it. The passive tags and cards we supply are exempt field devices, so the ETA obligation lands on the reader, which typically comes from your PACS or RTLS vendor. Every shipment we send carries full export documentation for Indian customs (commercial invoice, packing list, certificate of origin, Bill of Lading/Airway Bill). Network-connected reader hardware may also fall under TEC's MTCTE and BIS registration — your integrator handles those for the reader estate.

faq.question: What is the typical delivery time to India?
faq.answer: Express air freight from Shenzhen to Mumbai, Delhi, Bangalore, or Chennai takes 5-7 business days. With standard production of 5-7 business days, most orders arrive within 10-14 days of confirmation. Sea freight to Nhava Sheva, Chennai, or Kolkata takes 12-18 days and suits bulk shipments of 50,000+ units.

faq.question: Can you supply MIFARE cards compatible with Delhi Metro and other Indian transit systems?
faq.answer: Yes. Indian metro systems use MIFARE cards — typically MIFARE Classic 1K and MIFARE Ultralight, with MIFARE DESFire for higher-security programs. We manufacture these MIFARE smart cards in volume and can supply blank cards or custom-printed cards (ISO/IEC 14443) for the encoding systems used by Indian transit operators, campuses, and institutions.

faq.question: How do import duty and taxes work for Indian buyers?
faq.answer: India has no free-trade agreement with China, so imports get no preferential tariff: Basic Customs Duty (BCD) plus Integrated GST (IGST) apply at the border, and RFID cards and tags fall in the HS 8523.52 ("smart cards") family. The exact BCD and IGST depend on the precise HS classification and the current Union Budget, so we quote the landed figure against your specification rather than publish a rate. IGST paid at import is generally creditable for a GST-registered importer, which is why many Indian buyers import on their own IEC (Importer-Exporter Code) using FOB or CIF; DDP is available if you would rather we manage the border. Confirm the exact figures with your customs broker.

faq.question: What is the minimum order quantity for Indian buyers?
faq.answer: MOQs match our standard factory minimums: custom-printed PVC cards start at 500 pieces (digital printing accepts runs as low as 100), NFC inlays and labels at 1,000 pieces (one roll), and silicone wristbands at 500 pieces. Recurring production programs typically run 1,000-5,000 pieces per SKU. Free samples for compatibility and quality testing ship before any commitment.

brief.label: India band and radio rules
brief.text: UHF RFID in India operates in the 865-867 MHz band, de-licensed for RFID by the WPC (Wireless Planning & Coordination) wing of the Department of Telecommunications under GSR 564(E): no licence is needed to possess or operate RFID on a non-interference, non-protection, shared basis at up to 1 W transmitter (conducted) power, 4 W ERP, and 200 kHz carrier bandwidth. Because 865-867 MHz falls inside the EU 865-868 MHz band, EU-tuned inlays perform in India; US 902-928 MHz inlays read short. HF NFC and access cards at 13.56 MHz are globally harmonised and unaffected.

brief.label: Equipment approval (WPC ETA, TEC, BIS)
brief.text: RFID readers are intentional radiators and require WPC ETA (Equipment Type Approval) before they can be imported or cleared through Indian customs; network-connected telecom equipment additionally falls under TEC's Mandatory Testing and Certification (MTCTE), and BIS registration covers product safety. Passive UHF and NFC tags backscatter the reader's field, sit below the radio threshold, and are exempt field devices — so the approval obligation lands on the reader, not the tag or card.

brief.label: Landed cost
brief.text: India has no free-trade agreement with China, so imports get no preferential tariff: standard Basic Customs Duty (BCD) plus Integrated GST (IGST) apply at the border. RFID cards and tags classify in the HS 8523.52 ("smart cards") family. Exact BCD and IGST depend on the precise HS line and the current Union Budget, so we quote the landed figure rather than publish a rate — and many Indian buyers import on their own IEC (Importer-Exporter Code) to reclaim IGST as input credit.
